---
title: "8 · Evaluation of the soil state"
---

Every number here is tagged with its **basis** — a genuinely independent test, a shared-forcing
consistency check, or a synthetic demonstration — because the value of a score depends entirely on
which it is ([Evaluation data](02-evaluation-data.qmd)).

## The observing networks, and what each one can say

Four ground networks are **employed** today — actually ingested and assimilated — and are **not
interchangeable**: each constrains a different term, and a model can be badly wrong in a way that only
one of them can see. A second set is **planned**: real, located networks with no fetcher or
assimilation path in this repo yet. [The network map](#fig-network-map) marks the two sets with black
vs. gray marker edges, and that same `employed` flag is the single source of truth
(`ObsStream.employed` in `src/models/observability.py`) read by every figure in this chapter.

| network | status | observes | constrains |
|---|---|---|---|
| **NWIS wells** | employed | the hydraulic head of the **screened interval**, at a point — depth to water only where that interval brackets the phreatic surface | the **saturated store** — state, and its seasonal amplitude and phase. Only sites classified `measurement_target == water_table` may enter as direct $h_{wt}$/DTW observations ([assimilation](04-assimilation.qmd#which-wells-actually-observe-the-water-table)) |
| **USGS gauges** | employed | streamflow, integrated over a basin | the **fluxes** — runoff, interflow, baseflow, via a hydrograph separation |
| **SNOTEL** | employed | SWE and soil moisture, at a point | the **snowpack** — the recharge clock, and the vadose store |
| **Seismic (UW/CC)** | employed | dv/v, over a *volume* between stations | shallow **moisture change**, at storm timescales |
| **GHCN-Daily weather stations** | planned | precipitation, at a point | a local correction/downscaling target for the coarse gridded precip products (the same role these stations already play in PRISM) |
| **GNSS-IR / GNSS-TEC** | planned | precipitable water in the atmosphere, at a point | an independent atmospheric-moisture proxy for the forcing side of the water budget, not the soil state itself |
| **NOAA Stage IV radar precip** | planned | precipitation, 4 km gridded, domain-wide | a higher-cadence alternative/complement to the static gridded precip forcing |
| **Sentinel surface water** | planned | inundated water extent, geospatially distributed | best read as a **time-lapse** product — geospatially distributed water height/extent at a ~weeks repeat, not a station network with discrete sites |

::: {.callout-note}
## Seismic stations can double as streamflow gauges
Band-limited seismic power tracks turbulent flow and hence discharge, so a subset of the UW/CC
stations already used for dv/v can, in principle, also serve as a **streamgage proxy**
[@denolle2026seishydro]. That paper's finding for this same region is specific: the seismic-power–to–
discharge relationship stays robust through a compound atmospheric-river flood, but the interesting
signal is the *deviation* between the seismic proxy and the real gauge, which grows specifically during
intense AR events rather than gradually — i.e. the proxy is most informative exactly where a nearby real
gauge is most valuable to have, not as a wholesale substitute for one. This is marked on
[the network map](#fig-network-map) as a gray dashed halo on the seismic markers, not a new point set:
it is the same physical stations, evaluated for a second use.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Wells alone cannot validate a water budget
The state can be reproduced while the **flux partition** is badly wrong, because nothing in a
depth-to-water record sees where the water went. Streamflow does: it *is* the catchment water budget
integrated over a basin, and a baseflow separation splits it into quickflow and groundwater discharge.
The gauges are therefore not a secondary check on the wells — they constrain a different half of the
problem, and the calibration uses both ([Physics — Hydrology](03a-physics-hydrology.qmd)).
:::

## dv/v: a forward prediction everywhere, a measurement over a volume

::: {.callout-warning}
## The twin's dv/v field is a model output, not an observation
The twin evaluates `dvv_high` and `dvv_low` at **every 90 m cell**. That field is a **forward
prediction**: it is computed from the modelled soil moisture and water table through the petrophysical
coupling ([Physics — Hydromechanics](03b-physics-hydromechanics.qmd)), and it exists wherever the model
exists.

A **measured** dv/v does not live at a cell. It is a property of a **station pair**: the coda of the
noise cross-correlation samples the medium over an extended region, with a sensitivity that is a
spatial kernel rather than a point. Displaying the modelled field everywhere without saying so would
imply the network measures it everywhere.
:::

For diffuse coda, the sensitivity of the travel-time change between receivers $r_1, r_2$ at lapse time
$t$ to a perturbation at $s$ is [@pacheco2005time]

$$
K(s) = \frac{\int_0^t p(r_1, s, u)\, p(s, r_2, t-u)\, \mathrm{d}u}{p(r_1, r_2, t)},
\qquad
p(r,t) = \frac{1}{4\pi D t}\, e^{-r^2/(4Dt)},
$$

with $p$ the intensity Green's function of the diffusion equation. Summing over the available pairs
gives the **network sensitivity** $S(x)=\sum_{\text{pairs}} K_{\text{pair}}(x)$
(`src/models/dvv_sensitivity.py`). Treating pairs as independent observations of the local
perturbation, the uncertainty of a dv/v-derived state scales as

$$\sigma(x) \;\propto\; \big[\,S(x)\,\big]^{-1/2},$$

so a cell with no sensitivity receives **no constraint at all** and falls back on the model — it is
returned as *no constraint*, not as a large-but-finite number that invites interpolation.

This is the **spatial** complement to the *depth* sensitivity of the coda (`codameter.uq_depth`, a
Rayleigh-kernel band matrix). Together they state *where* and *at what depth* a dv/v measurement carries
information. Both limits are real:

- **Depth support.** The shallowest realistic ambient-noise band peaks near ~45 m, below the top-30 m
  Vs30 window, so the Vs30 response to a shallow signal is diluted by the 30 m average — a depth-
  resolution limit, not a tuning artefact.
- **Spatial support.** Sensitivity concentrates near the stations and along the paths between them, and
  broadens with lapse time. Where the network is sparse, a dv/v measurement cannot test the twin.

::: {.callout-note}
## dv/v complements the wells and the soil-moisture sensors; it does not replace them
A well observes the **saturated store** at a point. SNOTEL observes the **vadose store** at a point.
The coda samples a **volume**, and its shallow band responds to moisture on the timescale of individual
storms — which the wells cannot see, because the water table *integrates* storms rather than resolving
them ([Forecast](06-forecast.qmd)).

The three are therefore complementary in **state**, in **support**, and in **timescale**. dv/v is the
right instrument for short-lead, event-scale validation of the moisture state; the wells and gauges are
the right instruments for the cumulative antecedent state and the flux partition.
:::

## Observability: variance reduction and information gain

The sensitivity map says *where an instrument responds*. The design question is sharper: **how much
does each network actually reduce the uncertainty of the state, and where?** This is a linear-Gaussian
inverse problem (`src/models/observability.py`). The state is an **anomaly about the deterministic
baseline** — the water-table-head anomaly $\Delta h_{wt}$ (equivalently, up to sign, the DTW anomaly),
or the soil-moisture anomaly — and it carries a Matérn prior of correlation length $L$, which is the
model's own *error* covariance and **not** a claim that absolute WTD is a stationary Gaussian field
([assimilation](04-assimilation.qmd#the-prior-lives-on-the-residual-not-on-the-absolute-water-table-landscape)).
Each sensor is a linear functional of that anomaly: a **point** operator for a well or a SNOTEL site,
and a **footprint** operator — the coda kernel — for dv/v. The two states are observed by different
instruments:

$$\Delta h_{wt} \;\leftarrow\; \text{water-table wells (point)} + \text{dv/v deep band (volume)},
\qquad
\Delta\theta \;\leftarrow\; \text{SNOTEL (point)} + \text{dv/v shallow band (volume)}.$$

From the Gaussian posterior covariance $C_\text{post} = C - CG^\top(GCG^\top + C_d)^{-1}GC$ we read,
per cell, the **variance-reduction ratio** $R = 1 - C_\text{post}/C \in [0,1]$ (the fraction of prior
variance the network removes), the **information gain** $\tfrac12\ln(C/C_\text{post})$ in nats, and the
**marginal gain** of one network beyond another, $R(A\cup B) - R(B)$.

::: {.callout-important}
## "Resolution" here means variance reduction, and that is not spatial resolving power
$R(j) = 1 - \mathrm{Var}_\text{post}(j)/\mathrm{Var}_\text{prior}(j)$ is a **fractional posterior
variance reduction at cell $j$**. It is a useful and honest quantity, and it is what every map in this
section shows. It is *not*, by itself, evidence that the state is resolved at 90 m.

The distinction bites hardest exactly where this chapter leans hardest on dv/v. A coda kernel averages
over kilometres; pushed through the update it can drive $R$ above 0.9 at a 90 m cell while the
estimate at that cell is a broad volume average. Variance fell; localization did not follow.

What answers the resolving-power question is a row of the **Bayesian resolution (averaging-kernel)
operator** $A = CG^\top(GCG^\top+C_d)^{-1}G$, whose row $j$ is $\partial\hat m_j/\partial m$ — the
weighting over the *true* field that the estimate at $j$ actually forms. `src/models/observability.py`
exposes three diagnostics built on it: `averaging_kernel()` (the rows themselves),
`resolution_width_km()` (the $|A_{j\cdot}|$-weighted RMS distance from cell $j$ — an effective
localization width), and `degrees_of_freedom_for_signal()` ($\mathrm{tr}\,A$ — how many independent
things the whole observing system determines, bounded by the number of observations). A unit test
constructs the exact trap: two observations with $R > 0.9$ at the same cell whose averaging widths
differ by more than an order of magnitude.

The function is still called `resolution()` for backward compatibility — every figure and notebook in
this chapter calls it — but it is an alias of `variance_reduction_ratio()`, and the quantity is the
ratio. **Do not read a high diagonal variance reduction as 90 m localization.**
:::

![**Observability of the twin, static layers and USGS gauges included.** Rows: GWL (top), soil
moisture (bottom). Columns: the static layers alone (see below); the point network alone; dv/v alone;
**the resolution dv/v adds beyond the point network**; USGS streamflow gauges, each footprint widened
to a Gaussian blob sized by that gauge's real drainage area (a basin-integrated flux is not a point
measurement — this is a stated geometric approximation, not a DEM-derived watershed polygon); and the
total information gain, now from static layers **and** network together, via the nonstationary-prior
construction described
[below](#the-static-layers-resolve-space-the-sensor-network-resolves-the-rest). The point sensors
resolve their own neighbourhoods — wells the lowland, SNOTEL a set of isolated blobs — and leave the
space between them unobserved. dv/v, a *volume* measurement, fills that space, contributing most
**exactly where the point sensors cannot reach**: the mountain headwaters for GWL, and the whole
between-station field for soil moisture. Gauges add resolution too, but only in small, localized blobs
at their own basin outlets — they mostly constrain **GWL**, not soil moisture directly, which is why
the SM row's gauge column is a gray placeholder rather than a map: gauges are not wired into this
design as an SM constraint, even though soil moisture and the water table are physically coupled
(they just do not correlate cell-for-cell the way a shared sensor would need). GWL's static-layer
column is genuinely patchy — HAND/soil covariates resolve real 90 m structure everywhere, not only near
wells — while soil moisture's is honestly **flat**: Stage 1 for SM is a pedotransfer envelope, not a
fitted regression, so its uncertainty is one constant, not a spatially validated one, and its
information-gain column is dominated by that unvalidated constant rather than genuine spatial skill —
a limitation to fix, not to hide.](assets/observability.png){#fig-observability}

Three results the maps make concrete:

- **Soil moisture is almost unobserved off-station.** SNOTEL is a handful of points; between them the
  prior is unconstrained. dv/v is the *only* network that resolves the soil-moisture field over an
  area, which is the quantitative form of the earlier statement that dv/v *complements* the point
  sensors rather than duplicating them.
- **dv/v extends GWL observation into the ungauged mountains.** Wells sit in the lowland; the marginal-
  gain panel shows dv/v adding resolution precisely in the headwater terrain where wells are absent and
  where the baseline water table is an extrapolation (the applicability-domain caveat below).
- **The design is legible.** Because the variance-reduction ratio is scale-free, these maps depend
  only on the correlation length, the smoothness and the instrument noise-to-prior ratios — not on the
  absolute prior variance — so they read as *where each network is worth its cost*, and where a new
  station would add the most. They do **not** read as maps of spatial resolving power, for the reason
  in the callout above; the dv/v columns in particular are the ones to read as "variance fell here",
  not "the field is resolved here".

::: {.callout-note}
## What is prior, and what is calibratable — all of it is calibratable
An earlier version of this callout described the correlation lengths and prior variances as "physical
inputs, not fits". That was too strong. $\sigma$, $L$ and $\nu$ are **prior hyperparameters**:
informed by physics and literature, but uncertain and ultimately to be calibrated from the twin's
out-of-fold residuals and held-out observations. The current values —
$L_\text{GWL} = 12$ km, $L_\text{SM} = 8$ km, in this repo's $\sqrt{2\nu}$ range convention — are
**provisional**, not measured physical constants, and under fixed-domain asymptotics $\sigma$ and $L$
are not even separately identifiable [@zhang2004inconsistent]. The *ordering*
$L_\text{GWL} > L_\text{SM}$ is the defensible part; the numbers are placeholders pending
`scripts/calibrate_spatial_prior.py`, whose machine-readable artifact these chapters are meant to cite
instead ([assimilation](04-assimilation.qmd#the-calibration-experiment-that-is-supposed-to-settle-this)).

The per-instrument noise is on the same footing: the deep dv/v band is a weaker, noisier handle on the
water table than a well and the shallow band a moderate handle on moisture, but the numbers should be
set from the network's *measured* performance, not asserted. The maps' *pattern* is robust to all of
this; the absolute variance reduction is not.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## The prior is Matérn on the *anomaly*, and its barrier mask is an approximation, not a truth
`GaussianPrior` defaults to a Matérn-3/2 correlation (once-differentiable), not the earlier
squared-exponential (issue #163) — a stationary Gaussian random field is smoother ($C^\infty$) than a
terrain-driven head or moisture *residual*, which has kinks at drainage divides and lithologic
contacts, actually is. What $\nu$ means, why the water-table anomaly and soil moisture must **not**
share a value, why $\nu = 3/2$ is a working hypothesis rather than a literature constant, and what is
identifiable from an infill network are all set out in
[the assimilation chapter](04-assimilation.qmd#the-spatial-prior-what-it-is-on-and-what-its-parameters-are-worth).

The prior also takes an optional per-cell `region_id` (aliased `barrier_id`) that forces correlation to
zero across labels, so a ridge cell and a valley cell 90 m apart are not implicitly assumed to
communicate just because they are close in Euclidean distance. Its status needs stating plainly: this
is a **hydrographic localization / barrier approximation**, not an exact physical covariance boundary.
A surface drainage divide is not necessarily a groundwater divide — groundwater crosses topographic
basin boundaries wherever aquifer geometry and hydraulic gradient say it does, and whether the water
table follows topography at all is conditional on recharge and transmissivity
[@haitjema2005subdued]. A hard zero is an infinitely strong statement about a boundary that is usually
partial. Preferred labels are therefore the **hydrogeologic domains** of
`src/features/hydrogeologic_domains.py` rather than drainage basins, and a *soft* connectivity weight
is the better long-term construct (#163, #188, #192). The figures above do not yet pass a label in, so
they still assume within-domain isotropy. The masking is **implemented** at the coarsened assimilation
grid the twin actually solves on (`notebooks/make_twin_gif.py`); the dense $(n,n)$ `C` is not tractable
at the full 90 m domain.

**Planned** (milestone: Applied math — DA estimator correctness): an operator-form representation that
supplies $\mathrm{diag}(B)$, $BG^\top$ and $GBG^\top$ without ever forming $B$ (#154/#163). Note that
the *classical local* sparse GMRF/SPDE construction exists only for integer $\alpha$, hence integer
$\nu$, so adopting it as prototyped would silently change $\nu = 1.5 \to 1$; rational SPDE methods
reach general smoothness [@bolin2020rational]. Either way the choice of numerical backend must follow
the statistical model, not select it.
:::

## The static layers resolve space; the sensor network resolves the rest

The variance-reduction maps above answer "how much does the **sensor network** reduce variance relative to
a spatially flat prior" — by construction they credit zero spatial information to HAND, soil
texture, or terrain, because that flat prior has no spatial structure of its own. But
[the structural model](00-structural-model.qmd#the-baseline-water-table-observation-anchored-not-assumed)'s
random forest already resolves real 90 m spatial structure from covariates alone, in cells with no
well anywhere nearby — the sensor-only maps are blind to that.

The fix reuses the same information-theoretic machinery, not a new one: the covariate-informed
estimate is treated as a **virtual self-observation of every cell** — footprint = identity, noise
= the random-forest tree-ensemble $\sigma_{\text{rf}}(x)^2$ already computed for the baseline's own
uncertainty budget. That puts "resolution from static layers" in exactly the same units as
"resolution from sensors," so the two are directly comparable and combinable through one
nonstationary prior $C(x,x') = \sigma_{\text{rf}}(x)\,\sigma_{\text{rf}}(x')\,\rho(|x-x'|)$ — the
same Matern correlation above, just scaled by the covariate-informed std at each point instead of a
constant.

::: {.callout-note}
## How the two resolutions are actually combined
Scaling a stationary correlation $\rho(x,x')$ by a *spatially varying* marginal std at each point is
the standard geostatistical "nonstationary variance, stationary correlation" construction — it stays
a valid covariance (positive semi-definite) for any $\rho$ that is, and it is exactly what makes the
two resolutions combinable rather than merely comparable. Treating $C_{\text{static}}$ as the prior
and then running the ordinary `blue_update`/`resolution` machinery with the sensor network as $G$
is **sequential Bayesian updating** — prior from static layers, likelihood from sensors — which is
mathematically identical to one joint update of a single "virtual observation per pixel + real
sensor rows" system, but far cheaper: it needs one $n\times n$ solve with the sensor footprints,
never an $n\times n$ system with one row per grid cell for the static layers too. Three
variance-reduction ratios fall out of the same $C_{\text{static}}$, differing only in which variance
sits in the denominator:

- $R_{\text{static}}(x) = 1-\sigma_{\text{rf}}(x)^2/\sigma_{\text{flat}}^2$ — static layers against
  a flat (no-covariate, no-well) prior;
- $R_{\text{combined}}(x) = 1-\mathrm{Var}_{\text{post}}(x)/\sigma_{\text{flat}}^2$ — static layers
  *and* sensors, still against the flat prior, where $\mathrm{Var}_{\text{post}}$ comes from solving
  `resolution(C_static, G_sensors, noise_sensors)`;
- $R_{\text{marginal}}(x) = 1-\mathrm{Var}_{\text{post}}(x)/\sigma_{\text{rf}}(x)^2$ — the same
  posterior, but measured against the static-layer prior instead of the flat one, i.e. what the
  sensor network adds *given that the static layers are already known*. This is the map a sensor-
  siting decision actually needs, and it is the per-cell analogue of `marginal_resolution()`
  elsewhere in this chapter — the only difference is that "the base network" here is the static-layer
  prior itself, not another sensor set.
:::

![**Where spatial resolution comes from, for the water table.** Static layers alone (top left)
resolve real but patchy structure everywhere, including far from any station — HAND/soil texture
do not care where the wells are. Wells + dv/v alone (top right) resolve smooth, station-centred
blobs that vanish in station-sparse terrain. Combined (bottom left) is their union. The bottom-right
panel is the one the sensor-design question actually needs: what the network adds **beyond** what
the static layers already give, evaluated against the covariate-informed prior rather than a flat
one — it is near zero in the sparse east (the network has nothing to add there) and largest in the
well-dense lowland (where it has the most to add). Regenerate with
`pixi run static-resolution-figure`.](assets/static_resolution.png){#fig-static-resolution}

The aggregate version of the top-left panel is the spatial-block-CV $R^2$ already reported in
`block_cv_metrics.json` — "how much spatial variance do the static layers explain when tested at
*unseen* locations" is the scalar summary of the same question this figure maps spatially.

### Satellite and surface-water streams

Two distributed observations enter the same design and change it qualitatively, because they observe
where the ground networks cannot — everywhere, rather than at sites.

- **Satellite soil moisture — a retrieval, not a measurement.** **SMAP** (L-band radiometer, 9 km) and
  the planned **NISAR** (L-band SAR, ~0.2 km) do not *measure* soil moisture; they retrieve it by
  inverting brightness temperature or radar backscatter through a retrieval model, so each is a
  spatially-resolved *estimate* carrying retrieval and vegetation/roughness error. What they uniquely
  provide is **coverage, not accuracy** — a domain-wide constraint where the ground networks are sparse.
  Because the variance-reduction ratio is scale-free, a not-yet-flown product can be evaluated for the
  coverage it *would* provide.
- **Surface-water extent.** Optical differencing (e.g. Sentinel-2 NDWI) maps inundation, which is the
  **variable source area** — the valley floors and riparian corridors (HAND $\approx 0$) where the
  water table outcrops and quickflow is generated. It is the *spatial* complement to the gauges: a gauge
  measures the basin-integrated discharge, surface-water extent shows *where* that discharge is
  generated, and it pins the shallow water table along the drainage network.

![**The full observing system.** Resolution of the state as each network is added — point (wells,
SNOTEL), volume (dv/v), satellite (SMAP now, NISAR future), and surface water. Top (soil moisture):
SNOTEL is a scatter of points; **SMAP fills the whole domain** at moderate resolution; dv/v adds local
detail; NISAR would approach full resolution. Bottom (groundwater): wells resolve only the lowland;
dv/v reaches the mountains; **surface-water extent lights up the entire drainage network**, the
flux-generating variable source area whose discharge the gauges see only as a basin integral.](assets/observing_system.png){#fig-observing-system}

The observing system is therefore layered by **support**: point sensors anchor specific sites,
satellites blanket the domain at their native resolution, dv/v samples the volume between stations, and
surface water traces the channel network. No single stream is sufficient, and the information-gain
maps show precisely where each one earns its place — which is also the basis for **where a new station,
or a new mission, would add the most**.

### The temporal axis — coverage is not enough for a fast state

Spatial resolution is only half the design. A state that changes fast is observed well only by a stream
that **samples** fast. Soil moisture decorrelates in days — a storm wets the ground and it drains within
a week — so a satellite that revisits weekly **aliases** the very events it exists to capture, however
fine its pixels. The water table integrates months, so a coarse revisit costs it little. The same sensor
is therefore worth different amounts for the two states.

For a state with temporal correlation time $\tau$, a stream sampling at interval $\Delta t$ resolves a
fraction $\rho(\Delta t)^2=\exp(-2\Delta t / \tau)$ of its variability under the OU model
(`ou_correlation`/`temporal_resolution`, [assimilation chapter](04-assimilation.qmd)), and a stream's
observability of a *dynamic* field is the product $R_\text{space}\times R_\text{time}$
(`src/models/observability.py`).

![**The observing system on both axes.** Left: each stream in the spatial-support / revisit-interval
plane, with retrievals (satellites) as diamonds and measurements as circles. Streams above the
soil-moisture decorrelation line alias the storm signal. Right: for the *fast* soil-moisture state, the
temporal resolution discounts the coverage — a weekly satellite's fine pixels fall to a fraction of
their nominal worth, while the continuous seismic array and the hourly probes keep theirs. **Great
space is not great time.**](assets/observing_spacetime.png){#fig-spacetime}

This is the quantitative form of "dv/v sees the storm; the water table integrates it": the seismic array
and the sub-daily in-situ probes carry the *temporal* information a satellite cannot, while the satellite
carries the *spatial* coverage they cannot. The design is complementary on **both** axes at once.

## Water-budget evaluation — fluxes and state together

The calibrated budget is scored against both observation classes simultaneously, with each parameter
pinned by a different one ([Physics — Hydrology](03a-physics-hydrology.qmd)):

| | model | observed | basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| baseflow index | 0.52 | 0.47 | **independent** — Lyne–Hollick separation, 6 gauges |
| runoff coefficient $Q/P$ | 0.71 | 0.57–0.73 | **independent** — per-basin closure |
| water-table seasonal amplitude | 1.02 m | 1.06 m | **independent** — 26,816 shallow-well observations |
| water-table peak month | 5 | 4 | **independent** — same wells |
| basin runoff / snow (SWE) | — | ERA5-Land | **cross-check** — independent forcing+model, all three faces at once |

Precipitation is averaged over each gauge's **own watershed** (NLDI polygons). The gauged basins are
Cascade headwater catchments receiving far more orographic precipitation than a domain mean, and
comparing basin discharge against domain-mean rainfall is not a closure. Comparison against wells is
likewise made **at the well locations**: wells are drilled where people live and are not a random sample
of the terrain.

## Groundwater-level evaluation

The baseline is scored by **spatial block cross-validation** with variogram-sized blocks, so nearby
wells never appear in both train and test folds: **block-CV RMSE ≈ 19 m**. A random split would leak,
because lowland wells cannot vouch for mountain cells.

::: {.callout-caution}
## The training wells do not sample the terrain the model must predict
The wells sit in the flat lowland (median slope 3.1°, 1% on ground steeper than 20°); the domain is
37% steep. A tree ensemble asked to predict there does not extrapolate — it returns the nearest
training leaf, so a ridge inherits a lowland water table with a small, confident, and meaningless
variance.

The baseline therefore carries an explicit **applicability domain**: confidence is the distance in
*standardised covariate space* to the nearest training well, not a spatial distance — a cell 200 m from
a well but 30° steeper than anything in training is an extrapolation. It flags **44% of the domain** as
low-confidence, where a physical (TOPMODEL) prior is blended in. The confidence field ships with the
water table; the ensemble spread is documented as a **lower bound** off-sample.
:::

## Soil-moisture evaluation — consistency versus independence

Two comparisons with very different meanings:

- Against **MERRA-2** root-zone reanalysis — a *model evaluation dataset* — the model tracks at
  domain-mean **r = 0.85** (bias −0.08 m³ m⁻³, RMSE 0.095). This is **inter-model agreement**, not
  validation.
- Against **ERA5-Land** — a *different* forcing and land-surface model (HTESSEL/ERA5) — the comparison
  is genuinely more independent than MERRA-2 or TerraClimate, and it uniquely tests soil moisture,
  runoff, and snow on the same grid. Where our snowmelt-driven recharge and ERA5-Land's diverge marks
  a real structural difference worth chasing, not a tuning residual.
- Against **in-situ SNOTEL** θ held out of the estimator — a *genuinely independent* reference — the
  pooled skill is markedly lower in the sparse Cascade uplands, exactly as an honest independent test
  should read. That gap is diagnostic rather than embarrassing: it localised missing physics.

## Snow evaluation

The degree-day module is scored against **30 SNOTEL SWE stations** in the domain (881–1414 m), fitted
on each station's own precipitation and temperature so that the rain/snow-line smearing of a 4 km
gridded product does not enter the calibration. The target is **melt-out timing** rather than SWE RMSE:
RMSE is dominated by the accumulation season, and minimising it selects a melt factor slow enough to
place melt release a month late.

## dv/v recovery — synthetic

The dv/v pipeline is validated end-to-end on a controlled synthetic with a *known* imposed velocity
change: coda-wave stretching recovers the banded $\delta v/v$ at **r > 0.95**, and the depth inversion
returns the imposed profile within its propagated covariance. This is a **synthetic demonstration** —
it establishes that the estimator is unbiased, not that the field measurement is.

## The digital-twin MVP metrics — what is skill and what is demonstration

The MVP summary has previously reported these five numbers side by side, with no way for a reader to
tell from a bare correlation coefficient whether it came from a held-out observation or from a signal
the pipeline was asked to recover in the first place. Tagged with **basis**, in the order they appear
in the MVP reporting:

| metric | value | reference | basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| groundwater baseline, block-CV RMSE | 18.5 m RMSE, $R^2 = 0.09$ (across 5 shuffle-split draws; $R^2$ sd 0.10, one draw negative) | held-out wells, pooled fixed-block fallback cross-validation — the `--domain`-absent branch of `src/models/baseline_regression.py`, not the per-domain variogram-block run (`data/processed/block_cv_metrics.json`, `pooled.rmse_mean = 18.49`) | **REAL** — the only row on this table scored against real observations withheld from fitting |
| soil moisture vs MERRA-2 | r = 0.85, bias −0.08, RMSE 0.095 | MERRA-2 root-zone reanalysis — the $r$ is the **domain-mean** correlation over $n=24$ monthly means (`domain_mean_r_rootzone = 0.8546`); the bias and RMSE are **per-cell**, pooled over the 4-cell domain (`root_zone`, whose own per-cell $r$ is 0.84). Two different aggregations, as `notebooks/validate_merra2.py` reports them | **MODEL cross-check** — another model's reanalysis; consistency, not validation (see above) |
| dv/v band recovery | r > 0.95 | controlled synthetic with a known imposed velocity change | **SYNTHETIC** — the inverse operator recovering the forward operator's own imposed signal; it shows the estimator recovers the imposed pattern, not that the field measurement does (see above) |
| assimilation posterior σ-reduction | 53% (WTD) / 91% (θ) | `data/processed/dvv_summary.json` (`assimilation.wtd_sigma_reduction = 0.529`, `assimilation.theta_sigma_reduction = 0.912`) | **SYNTHETIC** — a ratio of the model's own most-favourable σ cell against an *assumed prior* σ, not a truth comparison |
| attribution shares (near-station fraction) | ~94% wells (GWL), ~95% dv/v (soil moisture) | model introspection, [assimilation chapter](04-assimilation.qmd) | **SYNTHETIC** — precision-weight share of the near-station assimilation update, a function of the assumed σ's and station geometry; not an evaluation metric |

The MERRA-2 domain-mean monthly correlation is dominated by the shared seasonal cycle at $n=24$ months
over 4 cells; that is a small, coarse sample, not a spatially resolved test. The posterior σ-reduction
is not a skill metric at all: it has no truth comparison and no residual. It is $1 - \min\sigma /
\sigma_\text{prior}$ — the single most favourable cell in the model's own σ field — measured against a
hardcoded assumed prior σ (σ_prior = 0.5 m for WTD, 0.05 m³ m⁻³ for θ, hardcoded at
`old/notebooks/make_dvv_figures.py:180-182, 204-205`).
The attribution shares are the same kind of number: a precision-weight read-off with
no reference dataset and no residual, tabulated here only because it was previously reported alongside
skill numbers, not because it evaluates anything. (The separately-reported Vs30 attribution figure
is stale against the current summary artifact and is not restated here.)

This table covers the digital-twin MVP metrics specifically; the chapter's other evaluations —
water-budget, soil-moisture, snow — are in the sections above. Three MVP-adjacent numbers are
deliberately **not** tabulated: ERA5-Land (no committed comparison artifact), SNOTEL SWE melt-out
(an in-sample grid search, not a hold-out), and the SNOTEL independent θ comparison
(`notebooks/validate_snotel.py`: pooled $r$ 0.40 over 788 station-months, median seasonal $r$ 0.54 and
median anomaly $r$ 0.21 over 5 stations). Those three are different estimands from one run, not
competing estimates of one quantity, and none of them is a leave-one-station-out score — that script
holds nothing out, because nothing was ever fitted to SNOTEL θ. The repo's one genuine
leave-one-station-out score is a separate snow-phase quantity: `notebooks/calibrate_snow.py` refits
on four stations and scores the fifth, giving `loso_mean_r_calibrated = 0.439` in
`data/processed/snow_calibration.json`. Its companion `loso_mean_r_default = 0.493` is bit-identical
to `mean_r_default` — under the default parameters nothing is fitted, so there is nothing to hold out
and that figure is not an out-of-sample score. The calibrated parameters score $r = 0.499$ in-sample
but $0.439$ held-out: the tuning does not generalise.

**The SYNTHETIC rows are pipeline demonstrations, not skill.** They establish that the machinery runs
end to end and that the estimator recovers what it was given; they say nothing about how well the twin
tracks the real subsurface. Only the REAL row is a skill claim, and the MODEL cross-check row is a
consistency check against another model, not a validation.

::: {.callout-note}
## A number and a method pending reconciliation
The groundwater-level section above states block-CV RMSE ≈ 19 m; the committed artifact
(`data/processed/block_cv_metrics.json`, `pooled.rmse_mean = 18.49`) and the MVP reporting both give
18.5 m. The disagreement is not only in the digits: that section describes the score as coming from
variogram-sized blocks, whereas the committed artifact was written by the `--domain`-absent fallback
branch, which uses a fixed `--cv-block-km` default of 200 km and never consults a variogram range.
Neither the number nor the method is reconciled here.
:::

## Calibrated uncertainty

Uncertainty is calibrated, not decorative. From out-of-fold $(\mu, \sigma)$ we report empirical
**interval coverage** at the 50/80/90/95% levels, the **PIT** mean, and the **CRPS**. A product whose
stated $\sigma$ does not cover the observations at the nominal rate is recalibrated before release, so
the per-cell $\sigma$ that travels to the hazard models
([Hazard integration](07-hazard-integration.qmd)) means what it says.

Two uncertainties are reported separately and must not be conflated: the **model** uncertainty (the
spread of the estimate) and the **observability** (whether any instrument constrains that cell at all).
The dv/v sensitivity field above is the latter — a cell can have a confident model prediction and no
measurement able to test it.
